Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
The world is a dangerous place
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: The contamination appraisal is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of police violence in this profile. It is much more characteristic of sexual trauma or interpersonal violation with a strong disgust/shame component, and here there are no supporting memory, trigger, threat, or strategy items that would make this appraisal clinically coherent. The remaining items describe intrusive, alien, uncontrolled traumatic memory and general danger/body-reactivity beliefs, which fit severe PTSD, but the contamination item stands out as a trauma-incongruent appraisal.

vignette: As a police officer, Alexandra had always been proud of her ability to stay calm under pressure. But that changed on the night she was attacked by a fellow officer during a routine traffic stop. The sound of screeching tires and shattering glass still echoed in her mind like it was yesterday. When the memory came flooding back, as it often did without warning, Alexandra felt herself transported back to that chaotic scene. It wasn't just a mental image - she could smell the acrid scent of burning rubber, feel the searing pain of bruised ribs, and taste the metallic tang of fear on her lips. But what really unsettled her was how her body seemed to react as if she was still in danger, even when she knew she was safe. Her heart would pound, her palms grow sweaty, and her senses go on high alert - all for no reason at all. It made her feel like her own body had turned against her, a constant reminder that the world was indeed a treacherous place. As Alexandra struggled to make sense of these physical reactions, she couldn't shake off the feeling that she'd been betrayed by someone she trusted. That officer, who was supposed to be her partner and friend, had turned on her in an instant. As the days went by, Alexandra found herself avoiding anything that might trigger those memories - patrol routes that took her near the scene of the attack, police social events where she might run into her attacker's friends, even certain types of music that seemed to match the rhythm of her racing heartbeat. She started taking longer routes home from work, skipping shift changes with colleagues who asked too many questions about that night, and stopped attending community outreach programs that had once brought her so much joy. The isolation crept up on her slowly but inexorably - she was withdrawing into a world where memories haunted her at every turn. Yet, those memories remained stubbornly alien to her, as if they belonged to someone else's life rather than her own. She'd catch herself wondering what that person must have felt like during the attack, how they managed to survive such trauma. It was only when she forced herself back into the midst of it all - back to the scene, back to reliving those moments in all their sensory horror - that Alexandra realized just how far-reaching her negative appraisals had become. Her body reacted not because she was still in danger but because she believed, deep down, that she would never truly be safe again. That same nightmarish cycle of memory and appraisal played itself out time and again over the following months, until it seemed like every waking moment was spent on edge, waiting for another flashback to pounce. Her relationship with her partner began to fray at the edges - how could he possibly understand what she'd gone through? As the pressure mounted, Alexandra started questioning whether she even belonged in a job that had once brought her such pride and purpose. And yet, it was that very same job that now filled her with dread - every patrol car that passed seemed like a threat, every call to duty an ambush waiting to happen. It took a particularly brutal flashback during a routine traffic stop for Alexandra to finally acknowledge she needed help. She watched as the faces of frightened civilians blurred into the face of her attacker, and her mind went dark with panic. Something snapped inside - maybe it was her pride, or maybe it was just exhaustion from running on adrenaline fumes for so long. Whatever it was, Alexandra knew then that she couldn't keep living this way, trapped in a cycle of memories and appraisals that seemed designed to destroy everything good about her life. She made the call to seek help, scared but resolute - she would fight back against those demons, even if it meant confronting them head-on.
